readings.title: 6 ways to give that aren’t about money
body: Good news: You can be a generous person without writing a bunch of checks. In fact, many of the most awe-inspiring and effective examples of generosity are gifts of time and energy, talent and love, custom-fitted to a specific need. This type of giving is open to everyone.
Many of the most awe-inspiring and effective examples of generosity are gifts of time and energy, talent and love, custom-fitted to a specific need.

Not sure where to begin? Here are six gifts of time and attention that have the strong potential to spark ripple effects that affect millions, from head of TED Chris Anderson’s new book, Infectious Generosity .

Zen master Thich Nhat Hanh taught that attention is the most precious gift we can give someone. This is where generosity starts — with a willingness to stop focusing on ourselves and to instead pay attention to someone else and their needs. From that act of connection, anything can happen.

Truth is, it can be difficult. We spend much of our time lost in our own worlds. We are often reluctant to focus on the issues that others are dealing with. So we put up shields. And that means that many of the people who could really use our attention never feel seen by us. The generosity of attention is therefore the generosity of being willing to be a little uncomfortable, to take down those shields, to give up some time, to risk coming to care about someone else.
Whether you stop and have a meaningful connection with a person in need or spend 30 minutes researching a cause you think might matter, you have already begun your generosity journey.

In our connected era, there’s a type of generosity that matters more than ever: a willingness to reach out to those with whom we disagree with. Many disputes today play out in public online. Huge audiences can become glued to online feuds. What if we could bring a satisfying resolution to more of these conflicts?

It’s hard to reach out to our critics. This is a particularly challenging form of the generosity mindset. You are sacrificing your personal comfort for the greater good of bringing people together. But if you’re successful, there’s a powerful knock-on benefit: You are helping change the tone of public discussion today. That’s a gift to all of us.
The single greatest gift we can give is knowledge — knowledge that solves a problem, fills a need or opens a pathway forward.
In countless circumstances, the single greatest gift we can give is knowledge — knowledge that solves a problem, fills a need or opens a pathway forward.

Our single biggest piece of advice to someone coming to speak on the TED stage is to think of their talk not as an opportunity to pitch something (like a business or a cause) but rather as a gift. It is a chance to freely share valuable ideas with the audience. And those ideas have the potential to impact a listener’s life for years to come.

If you possess knowledge that others may benefit from, consider how you could share it to create ripple effects. What may take you a few hours to prepare and act on could light up someone’s life — and that could just be the beginning.

In our connected age, the networks we have access to matter more than ever. Therefore, one of the most important forms of viral generosity is to help people connect with others. The simplest way to do this is to make an introduction.

As psychologist and TED speaker Adam Grant has argued, an introduction can be fairly easy to give — and unbelievably valuable to receive. Ask many people how they met their partner, got their dream job or found the perfect collaborator for their creative project, and the answer will often be the same: someone — a friend, a neighbor, a colleague — introduced them to the right person. What you’re effectively doing is giving someone else access to your network of resources. And those introductions can have exponential consequences.

In his remarkable book Human Universals , anthropologist Donald Brown documented how hospitality is one of hundreds of human behaviors that have been observed in every single culture ever studied. But if hospitality is so ubiquitous (and so pleasant), is it really a form of generosity? Well, yes. Quite apart from any costs involved, it takes effort to invite someone over, whether friends or possible future friends. It’s easier just to watch the next episode of the TV series you’re into.
So how can hospitality contribute to infectious generosity? Hospitality taps into our deepest instincts for connection to one another. And each experience of it evokes a desire to reciprocate.
People need money, food, shelter and healthcare, to be sure. But we also yearn for beauty, wonder, laughter, transcendence — all elements of enchantment.

Pioneering artist Lily Yeh was approached by the dancer and choreographer Arthur L. Hall to undertake a community art project in a derelict, abandoned plot in her home city of Philadelphia. “I was interested but totally scared,” Yeh recalled. “I had little resources and no experience in working outdoors in a community setting. I wanted to run away, but I did not want to see a coward in the mirror. So I stepped into the project.”

The community project became the Village of Arts and Humanities, an art park full of trees, sculptures and mosaics created by local adults and children in collaboration with Yeh. Yeh’s work led her to a profound realization: that creating beauty in public spaces is profoundly healing and transformative for communities.

People need money, food, shelter and healthcare, to be sure. But we also yearn for beauty, wonder, laughter, transcendence — all elements of enchantment. Those who can enchant can offer a gift of immense value.

##段落

6种不花钱的给予方式
2024年1月22日
/
克里斯·安德森
Facebook

MINIWIDE / iStock
好消息：你不必写下一堆支票也能成为一个慷慨的人。事实上，许多最令人敬畏且最有效的慷慨之举，都是量身定制于特定需求的时间与精力、才华与爱心的馈赠。这种给予方式对每个人开放。

##段落
许多最令人敬畏且最有效的慷慨之举，都是量身定制于特定需求的时间与精力、才华与爱心的馈赠。

##段落
不知道从哪里开始？以下是六种时间与关注的馈赠，它们有巨大潜力激起涟漪效应，影响数百万人，内容源自TED负责人克里斯·安德森的新书《传染性慷慨》。

##段落
1. 转移关注
禅宗大师一行禅师教导说，关注是我们能给予他人最珍贵的礼物。这就是慷慨的起点——愿意停止关注自己，转而关注他人及其需求。从这种连接的行为出发，任何事情都可能发生。

##段落
事实上，这并不容易。我们大量时间迷失在自己的世界里。我们常常不愿去关注他人正在处理的问题。所以我们竖起盾牌。这意味着许多真正需要我们关注的人，从未感受到被我们看见。因此，关注的慷慨，就是愿意稍微不适、卸下那些盾牌、牺牲一些时间、冒险去在意他人的慷慨。

##段落
无论你是停下来与需要帮助的人建立一次有意义的连接，还是花30分钟研究一个你认为可能重要的议题，你都已经开始了你的慷慨之旅。

##段落
2. 架设桥梁
在我们这个互联的时代，有一种慷慨比以往任何时候都更重要：愿意主动接触那些与我们意见相左的人。如今许多争端在线上公开上演。大量观众可能会紧盯网络争斗。如果我们能为更多这类冲突带来令人满意的解决，会怎样？

##段落
主动接触批评者很难。这是慷慨心态中极具挑战性的一种形式。你是在为将人们聚在一起的更大善意而牺牲个人舒适。但如果你成功了，会有一个强大的附带好处：你在帮助改变当今公共讨论的基调。这是送给所有人的礼物。

##段落
我们能给予的最大礼物是知识——能够解决问题、满足需求或开辟前进道路的知识。

##段落
3. 分享知识
在无数情境中，我们能给予的最大礼物是知识——能够解决问题、满足需求或开辟前进道路的知识。

##段落
我们给某人的最大建议是

在TED舞台上发言，关键在于将自己的演讲视为一份礼物，而非推销某个项目（如事业或公益）的机会。这是一个与听众自由分享宝贵想法的契机，而这些想法有可能在未来数年影响听者的生活。
如果你拥有能让他人受益的知识，不妨思考如何分享它，以激起层层涟漪。你花几小时准备和行动的内容，或许能点亮某人的生活——而这可能仅仅是个开始。
4. 促成连接
在这个互联时代，我们所能触及的人脉网络比以往任何时候都更为重要。因此，病毒式慷慨最重要的形式之一，就是帮助人们与他人建立联系。最简单的方式便是引荐。
正如心理学家及TED演讲者亚当·格兰特所言，引荐对给予者来说轻而易举，对接受者却价值连城。问问许多人如何遇见伴侣、获得理想工作或为创意项目找到完美搭档，答案往往如出一辙：有人——朋友、邻居或同事——将他们引荐给了合适的人。你实际上是在让别人接入你的人脉资源网络，而这些引荐可能带来倍增的连锁效应。
5. 热情款待
人类学家唐纳德·布朗在其杰作《人类共通性》中，记录了热情款待如何成为所有被研究文化中普遍存在的数百种人类行为之一。但若热情好客如此普遍（且令人愉悦），它真算得上一种慷慨吗？答案是肯定的。且不论任何花费，邀请他人上门——无论是朋友还是潜在的新朋友——都需要付出心力。相比之下，刷下一集追的剧要轻松得多。
那么，热情款待如何助长传染性慷慨？它触及我们彼此联结的最深层本能，而每一次款待体验都会唤起回报的渴望。
人们确实需要金钱、食物、住所和医疗保健，但我们同样渴望美、惊奇、欢笑与超越——这些都是迷醉的元素。
6. 创造迷醉
先锋艺术家莉莉·叶受舞蹈家兼编舞家亚瑟·L·霍尔的邀请，在她家乡费城一片废弃荒芜的地块上开展社区艺术项目。“我感兴趣，但又完全害怕，”叶回忆道，“我资源匮乏，也没有在社区户外工作的经验。我想逃离，但不想在镜子里看到懦夫，所以我迈入了这个项目。”
这个社区项目后来成为“艺术与人文村”，一个由当地成年人

叶与儿童合作，叶的工作让她深刻领悟到：在公共空间创造美，对社区具有深远的治愈与变革力量。
人们当然需要金钱、食物、住所和医疗保健。但我们也渴望美、惊奇、欢笑与超越——这些都是魅力的要素。能带来魅力的人，能赠予极具价值的礼物。

readings.title: The Pacific warming patterns warping US weather
body: 34 minutes ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Isabelle Gerretsen A rare but powerful combination of an immense Pacific Ocean heatwave and a "super El Niño" are set to have profound effects on US weather and marine life this autumn. Here are five changes to expect. In the north-east Pacific Ocean, an immense and persistent heatwave is wreaking havoc on marine life and weather patterns. "It's a really bright red eyeball in the Pacific," says Andrew Leising, a research oceanographer at the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (Noaa). "It's huge, it stretches across the whole [ocean]." The Pacific heatwave, which formed in May 2025, is already bringing surface temperatures 3-4C (5.4-7.2F) above average for this time of year, according to Leising. Add to that: a massive warming pattern known as El Niño is brewing further south. El Niño is a weather phenomenon that pushes up global temperatures, and it is also supercharging Pacific Ocean warming. It is expected to intensify this autumn to become the strongest El Niño in living memory . This combination of a massive marine heatwave and a "super El Niño" is rarely seen. Here are five impacts we can expect to see – and where they will happen. California: More storm surges, intense floods California, which has been in the grips of a marine heatwave since December, is bracing for more storm surges and flooding over the autumn and winter due to warmer coastal waters. Coastal water levels are already 15cm (5.9in) above mean sea level, says Patrick Barnard, research director of the Center for Coastal Climate Resilience at the University of California, Santa Cruz. During this El Niño, that already high sea level will soar further still: to at least 15-30cm (5.9-11.8in) higher than normal, says Barnard. "Every 5-10cm [1.9-3.9in] of mean sea level rise doubles the flooding frequency for most coastal communities along the US West Coast, so with all these expected sea level increases peaking this winter, we will have historically high flood risk," he says. Warmer ocean surfaces also evaporate more heat and moisture into the air, which can cause heavier rainfall, says Leising. This can lead to more atmospheric rivers – huge, invisible ribbons of water vapour in the sky – in the coming months. These raise the risk of heavy inland flooding and mudslides in California too. What is El Niño? El Niño is a natural phenomenon which occurs when sea surface temperatures in the Pacific Ocean are 0.5C (0.9F) higher than normal for several consecutive months. When the increase is 2C (3.6F), a "very strong" or "super" El Niño occurs.   Pacific Northwest US and Canada: Less snowfall, risk of drought Further north in the US and in Canada, the combined impact of El Niño and marine heatwaves is expected to reduce snowfall, says Larry O'Neill, professor at Oregon State University and director of the Oregon Climate Service. The last huge Pacific marine heatwave, coined "the Blob", led to a record low snowpack in the Pacific Northwest in 2015 . "It may have modified the jet stream and sent storms further north than usual. The storms we did get were much warmer than usual, so the precipitation that would usually come as snow came as rain at higher elevations," says O'Neill. Reduced snowfall is a concern as many parts of the Pacific Northwest are currently experiencing drought conditions , he adds. "It could take multiple winters for us to recover." Dry conditions and above-average warming in the north-west US, exacerbated by El Niño, increase the risk of wildfires across northern California, eastern Oregon, southern Idaho and Utah this autumn. This is projected to reduce air quality for millions and result in billions of dollars of economic impact. Meanwhile in California, warmer coastal waters have already led to warmer, more humid conditions across the state over the spring and summer this year, according to Leising. In inland California, temperatures also tend to be "a little warmer", during a marine heatwave, as the winds off the ocean pick up a little extra heat before moving away from the coast, says Nick Bond, a climatologist at the University of Washington.   Fewer Atlantic hurricanes, more Pacific storms Over in the Atlantic Ocean, El Niño tends to suppress hurricane development as it makes thunderstorms less likely to become hurricanes. But tropical storms in the eastern Pacific are stronger as warmer ocean waters provide additional energy, with heightened risk for Mexico. These tropical storms can help weaken marine heatwaves during the autumn, says O'Neill. "Evaporation from the winds and the cold temperatures tends to cool [them] off." A 2020 study by O'Neill found that strong storms fully destroyed marine heatwaves in the Northeast Pacific in a matter of days between 2013 and 2016. The heatwave off California is already "basically cooking the animals along the coast", says Leising. During a marine heatwave, nutrients don't rise to the ocean surface as often as they usually do and oxygen levels in the water are lower, says O'Neil. "A lot of fish and shellfish will not have enough oxygen, so they'll either die or they'll go further offshore." Fisheries are likely to feel the effects of this damage to the ecosystem, he says. The only marine heatwave to beat the current one for size led to "really big changes in the marine ecosystem" , says Bond. " The Blob ", which lasted from 2013-16, stretched for 1,000 miles (1,609km) between North America and Asia. "Warm water species thrived at the expense of the cooler water species," says Bond. This was detrimental for juvenile salmon, for marine mammals and some sea birds, he adds. The heatwave in the Pacific is starting to become more or less a permanent feature of the climate system – Nick Bond The duration of these heatwaves is a major concern, says Leising. "Marine animals will have been exposed to this warm water for a really long time over a large area, and now they're just going to roll right into the warm waters from El Niño." Some species, such as rockfish and squid, may benefit from warmer waters, "but overall the balance is more losers as the productivity is down for the whole system", he says. "There's less food out there for everyone." Large marine heatwaves have occurred each of the past seven years and six of these were  among the biggest on record for the eastern North Pacific since records began in 1982. The increase in these marine heatwaves is directly linked to climate change, says O'Neill. "Marine heatwaves are occurring more frequently now, because the ocean has been warming unrelentingly over the last 40 years." More like this: •  The couple who married in typhoon floods •  How do you cool a 100F city? •  The most extreme hurricanes in history Since the 1970s, there has been a marked acceleration in sea surface temperatures and the ocean has absorbed more than 90% of the excess heat from climate change. Today, ocean temperatures are hotter than they have ever been . The heatwave in the northeast Pacific is "starting to become more or less a permanent feature of the climate system," says Bond. It is only the second time in recorded history that a marine heatwave of this magnitude has occurred alongside an El Niño, says Leising, noting that the relationship between these two events is not fully understood. Scientists are still working out how climate change influences El Niño , but agree that the frequency of these events is likely to increase this century due to global warming. Met Office forecasts suggest that sea surface temperature anomalies could exceed 3C (5.4F) later in 2026 as El Niño reaches its peak. El Niño events typically lasts 9-12 months , with this one expected to dissipate around spring. It is unknown how long the marine heatwaves will last. "They certainly do have some real persistence to them. The Blob had legs," says Bond. For as long as the waters of the Pacific Ocean remain excessively hot, we can expect the weather and marine life to feel the effects. -- For essential climate news and hopeful developments to your inbox, sign up to the Future Earth newsletter, while The Essential List delivers a handpicked selection of features and insights twice a week. For more science, technology, environment and health stories from the BBC, follow us on Facebook and Instagram . 34分钟前 分享 保存 设为Google首选 伊莎贝尔·格雷森 一场罕见但威力巨大的组合——太平洋巨大热浪与“超级厄尔尼诺”——预计将在今年秋季对美国天气和海洋生物产生深远影响。以下是值得关注的五个变化。在东北太平洋，一场巨大而持久的热浪正在对海洋生物和天气模式造成严重破坏。“这是太平洋上一个非常醒目的红色眼球，”美国国家海洋和大气管理局（Noaa）研究海洋学家安德鲁·莱辛说。“它巨大无比，横跨整个（海洋）。”据莱辛称，这场太平洋热浪于2025年5月形成，已经使海面温度比同期平均水平高出3-4摄氏度（5.4-7.2华氏度）。再加上：一种名为厄尔尼诺的大规模增温现象正在更南地区酝酿。厄尔尼诺是一种推高全球气温的天气现象，同时也在加剧太平洋变暖。预计它将在今年秋季增强，成为有生以来最强的厄尔尼诺。这种巨大海洋热浪与“超级厄尔尼诺”的组合极为罕见。以下是我们可以预期的五个影响——以及它们将发生在哪里。

##段落
加利福尼亚州：更多风暴潮、严重洪水 自12月以来一直受海洋热浪影响的加利福尼亚州，由于沿海水域变暖，预计在秋季和冬季将面临更多风暴潮和洪水。加州大学圣克鲁兹分校沿海气候韧性研究中心研究主任帕特里克·巴纳德表示，沿海水位已经比平均海平面高出15厘米（5.9英寸）。在本次厄尔尼诺期间，本已较高的海平面将进一步飙升：至少比正常水平高出15-30厘米（5.9-11.8英寸），巴纳德说。“平均海平面每上升5-10厘米（1.9-3.9英寸），美国西海岸大多数沿海社区的洪水频率就会翻倍，因此随着所有这些预期的海平面上升在今年冬季达到顶峰，我们将面临历史性的高洪水风险，”他说。莱辛指出，更温暖的海洋表面也会向空气中蒸发更多热量和水分，这可能导致更强的降雨。这将在未来几个月引发更多大气河——天空中巨大、无形的带状水蒸气。这些也会增加加利福尼亚州内陆严重洪水和泥石流的风险。什么是厄尔尼诺？厄尔尼诺是一种自然现象，当太平洋海面温度连续数月比正常水平高出0.5摄氏度（0.9华氏度）时发生。当增幅达到2摄氏度（3.6华氏度）时，就会出现“非常强”或“超级”厄尔尼诺。

##段落
美国太平洋西北部和加拿大：降雪减少、干旱风险 在美国更北部地区和加拿大，厄尔尼诺与海洋热浪的联合影响预计将减少降

俄勒冈州立大学教授、俄勒冈气候服务中心主任拉里·奥尼尔表示，海洋热浪可能导致积雪减少。上一次巨大的太平洋海洋热浪被称为“斑点”，在2015年导致太平洋西北地区的积雪量创下历史新低。奥尼尔说：“它可能改变了急流，使风暴比平时更向北移动。我们遇到的风暴比平时温暖得多，所以在较高海拔地区，通常以雪的形式出现的降水变成了雨。”他补充说，降雪减少令人担忧，因为太平洋西北部的许多地区目前正经历干旱状况。“我们可能需要多个冬天才能恢复。”美国西北部的干旱和高于平均水平的变暖，加上厄尔尼诺现象的影响，增加了今年秋天北加州、俄勒冈州东部、爱达荷州南部和犹他州发生野火的风险。预计这将降低数百万人的空气质量，并造成数十亿美元的经济影响。与此同时，莱辛表示，在加利福尼亚州，今年春夏两季，沿海水域变暖已经导致整个州出现更温暖、更潮湿的天气。华盛顿大学的气候学家尼克·邦德说，在内陆加州，海洋热浪期间的气温也往往“稍微暖和一点”，因为海风在离开海岸前会吸收一些额外的热量。

大西洋飓风减少，太平洋风暴增多在大西洋，厄尔尼诺现象往往会抑制飓风的形成，因为它使雷暴不太可能变成飓风。但东太平洋的热带风暴更强，因为更温暖的海水提供了额外的能量，对墨西哥的风险更大。奥尼尔说，这些热带风暴有助于在秋季减弱海洋热浪。“风的蒸发和低温往往会使其降温。”奥尼尔2020年的一项研究发现，在2013年至2016年期间，强风暴在几天内就完全摧毁了东北太平洋的海洋热浪。莱辛说，加州附近的海洋热浪已经“基本上在烹煮沿海的动物”。奥尼尔说，在海洋热浪期间，营养物质上升到海洋表面的频率不如平时，水中的氧气含量也较低。“很多鱼和贝类会没有足够的氧气，所以它们要么死亡，要么会游到更远的海域。”他说，渔业可能会受到生态系统破坏的影响。邦德说，唯一比当前海洋热浪规模更大的海洋热浪导致了“海洋生态系统的巨大变化”。“斑点”从2013年持续到2016年，在北美和亚洲之间延伸了1000英里（1609公里）。邦德说：“暖水物种以牺牲冷水物种为代价而繁盛。”这是有害的。

##段落
他补充道，这对幼年鲑鱼、海洋哺乳动物和一些海鸟来说尤为如此。太平洋的这次热浪正开始或多或少成为气候系统的永久特征——尼克·邦德。莱辛表示，这些热浪的持续时间是一个重大关切。“海洋动物将在很大范围内长时间暴露在温暖的水域中，而现在它们将直接进入厄尔尼诺带来的暖水中。”他说道，像岩鱼和鱿鱼这样的物种可能从较暖的水域中受益，“但总体而言，损失者更多，因为整个系统的生产力都在下降，”他说，“每个人可获得的食物都更少了。”过去七年中每年都发生了大规模海洋热浪，其中六次是自1982年有记录以来东北太平洋最大的热浪之一。奥尼尔表示，这些海洋热浪的增加与气候变化直接相关。“现在海洋热浪发生得更频繁了，因为过去40年来海洋一直在持续变暖。”更多相关内容：• 在台风洪水中结婚的夫妇• 如何为华氏100度的城市降温？• 历史上最极端的飓风。自20世纪70年代以来，海面温度显著加速上升，海洋吸收了气候变化中超过90%的多余热量。如今，海洋温度比以往任何时候都要高。邦德表示，东北太平洋的热浪“正开始或多或少成为气候系统的永久特征”。莱辛指出，这是有记录以来第二次如此规模的海洋热浪与厄尔尼诺同时发生，并强调这两者之间的关系尚未被完全理解。科学家们仍在研究气候变化如何影响厄尔尼诺，但一致认为，由于全球变暖，本世纪这类事件的发生频率可能会增加。英国气象局的预测表明，随着厄尔尼诺在2026年晚些时候达到峰值，海面温度异常可能超过3摄氏度（5.4华氏度）。厄尔尼诺事件通常持续9至12个月，预计此次将在春季左右消散。目前尚不清楚海洋热浪会持续多久。“它们确实具有一定的持久性。‘斑点’热浪是有‘腿’的，”邦德说。只要太平洋水域仍然异常炎热，我们就可以预期天气和海洋生物将感受到其影响。——如需获取重要的气候新闻和充满希望的发展动态，请订阅《未来地球》通讯，而《精选清单》每周两次为您提供精心挑选的专题和见解。如需更多来自BBC的科学、技术、环境和健康故事，请在Facebook和Instagram上关注我们。地球 气候 极端天气 洪水 海洋 环境

readings.title: Is Italy the new tax haven for the global rich?
body: 22 April 2026 Share Save Add as preferred on Google John Laurenson Italy has already been attacked by the French Government for using tax incentives to lure wealthy French and other international residents away, but with the war in the Middle East hurting the Gulf states, Italy has become an even more attractive location for the rich. Tax wasn't the main reason for leaving France, Robert insists over a café crème at Charles de Gaulle airport. It was the beauty of Italy, the bella vita  (the beautiful/good life), the art and the music. But for the Frenchman, buying a house in Rome and becoming an Italian tax resident was a very nice part of the package offered by the country, where high net worth individuals can pay a fixed annual tax on all foreign income – regardless of amount – and enjoy a series of other exemptions.  Robert, who describes himself as only "moderately wealthy", moved to Italy eight years ago after a career in computers which ended with him selling his company. Robert, not his real name, may not be among the French billionaires who have fled the French taxman for Italy, but the advantages to him are clear.   If he'd been buying a house in France, he would have had to pay what the French call frais de notaire (solicitor's fees) most of which goes to the government (much like Stamp Duty in the UK or Real Estate Transfer Taxes in the US). In Italy there's an exemption for the prima casa , the first house you buy. In France, President Macron transformed France's Impot sur la Fortune  (wealth tax) into an Impot sur la Fortune Immobilière  (real estate wealth tax) so stock market investments, for example, are no longer affected but "if you have ten million dollars' worth of property, this tax is very painful indeed," says Robert. Again, there's nothing like that in Italy.  In France you also have to pay a property tax ( taxe foncière or land tax). "We don't have that here for the prima casa (first home)," says Robert, although he notes "there is a high charge for refuse collection". The best thing as far as he is concerned is that there is no inheritance tax on property you own in Italy up to €1 million ($1.1 million) and it's only 4% beyond that threshold. In France the tax-free limit is much lower – €100,000 ($110,000) – and beyond that it's a sliding scale up to a top rate of 45%. But it's for the seriously rich that Italy starts to look like a fiscal paradise. "I have friends who have moved here for tax reasons and others who are thinking about it," Robert tells me. "For people who really pay a lot of tax, Italy is very attractive because of it's "flat tax". In Italy, the taxman fixes an upper limit of tax that can be levied on income. However much you earn, you never pay more than that. The upper limit is now €300,000 ($353,000). Although not long ago it was €100,000 before rising to €200,000. If you're paying a million euros of income tax a year in France, Italy is very tempting. As for US citizens, Americans are always taxable on worldwide income, so moving to Italy would not help their tax bill. Even at €300,000, Italy's flat tax is still low for anyone making over €1m per year compared to anywhere else in Europe – Peter Ferrigno Robert tells me that he has two rich French friends who have moved to Italy in the past few months, but they came from the UK. They were both working in finance in the City of London and were keen to move to a place where the fiscal regime was as sympathetic to them as the one Britain had before it changed the rules for wealthy foreign residents.  "Even at €300,000, Italy's flat tax is still low for anyone making over €1m per year compared to anywhere else in Europe. And it means you get tax certainty and clarity, within the heart of Europe, rather than having to go a long way," says Peter Ferrigno, director of tax services at wealth migration specialists Henley & Partners. "We have meetings with people every week who would like to leave France," says Paris-based tax lawyer Jerome Barre. "They are unhappy about the tax situation now and they are worried that it will become harsher in the future. People are not confident with the political climate. Taxes are changing a lot, almost every year. People are frightened that after the election of the new president in 2027, things could become harder than today," he says. At this stage though it's more "questions from entrepreneurs and wealthy people who are wondering if they would like to move or not move rather than people actually moving," Jerome Barre explains. "Relocation requires full commitment and careful structuring," he stresses. He adds that for business-owners  " they need to change the seat of the company. They are subject in France to an exit tax." If many wealthy French people are at the "thinking-about-moving" stage, the question is being felt even more acutely in the United Arab Emirates. It's inevitable that many people will reconsider UAE – Peter Ferrigno But giving up on Dubai's zero-tax regime will be very difficult for many. "When you are in a country where you do not pay any tax, it's very difficult to come back to a country where you have to pay a lot. Especially for those used to spending a lot of money. The net in your pocket is very different, says Barre. And, he adds, people who have grown used to the zero-tax life "are not used to administrative formalities anymore – tax returns, documents – so it's not easy." More like this: • Dubai's tourism industry reels from 'brutal' impact of war • Why more Americans are now moving to Ireland • Is New York's cannabis business really flying high? "It's inevitable that many people will reconsider UAE," says Henley & Partners' Peter Ferrigno. "But I think it's far too early for people to wholesale uproot their life when it involves work, family, etc. The vast majority of people in the UAE are still regular people doing regular jobs, even most of the millionaires are millionaires because they are doing well paid jobs rather than being asset owners. If the war is relatively short, they will remain. If it drags on, then people will inevitably look elsewhere, or relocate the family and work remotely until it's safer. If you're in the UAE for work, there aren't likely to be that many equivalent roles in Italy," he says. However, it is likely that the war in the Middle East will dissuade many rich Europeans who would have otherwise moved there from re-locating to the UAE. Last year, Dubai was the number one destination by far for migrating millionaires, according to Henley & Partners. That number is bound to tumble in 2026, and with its attractive offer for the very wealthy, as well as its reputation for  la dolce vita  of course, it may well be Italy that benefits. -- For global insights and expert analysis for the boardroom and beyond, sign up to the  World of Business newsletter , while  The Essential List  delivers a handpicked selection of features and insights.  For more on business and beyond, follow us on  LinkedIn . 2026年4月22日 分享 保存 设为Google首选 约翰·劳伦森 意大利已经因利用税收优惠吸引富有的法国及其他国际居民而受到法国政府的攻击，但随着中东战争冲击海湾国家，意大利对富人而言变得更加具有吸引力。罗伯特在戴高乐机场边喝咖啡边坚持说，离开法国的主要原因不是税收，而是意大利的美丽、美好生活、艺术和音乐。但对这位法国人来说，在罗马购房并成为意大利税务居民是该国提供的一揽子优惠中非常诱人的一部分，高净值人士可以就所有海外收入缴纳固定年度税款——不论金额多少——并享受一系列其他豁免。 自称仅“中等富裕”的罗伯特，在从事计算机行业并最终出售公司后，八年前移居意大利。罗伯特并非真名，他可能不属于逃离法国税务部门前往意大利的法国亿万富翁之列，但对他来说，好处显而易见。如果他在法国购房，就必须支付法国人所谓的公证费，其中大部分上缴政府（类似英国的印花税或美国的房地产转让税）。而在意大利，首套购房可享受豁免。在法国，总统马克龙将财富税转变为房地产财富税，因此股市投资等不再受影响，但“如果你拥有价值1000万美元的房产，这项税确实非常沉重，”罗伯特说。而意大利没有类似税种。 在法国，你还必须缴纳房产税（土地税）。“在意大利，首套住房无需缴纳这种税，”罗伯特说，尽管他提到“垃圾收集费很高”。在他看来，最好的地方在于，在意大利拥有的房产价值不超过100万欧元（110万美元）时无需缴纳遗产税，超出部分仅按4%征税。而法国的免税限额低得多——10万欧元（11万美元）——超出部分按累进税率最高达45%。但对于真正的超级富豪而言，意大利开始显得像税收天堂。“我有朋友因税收原因搬到这里，还有人在考虑此事，”罗伯特告诉我。“对于实际缴纳大量税款的人来说，意大利因其‘统一税’而极具吸引力。”在意大利，税务机关设定了收入征税的上限。无论你赚多少，缴纳的税款永远不会超过这个上限。目前上限为30万欧元（35.3万美元）。尽管

不久之前，这一数字还是10万欧元，随后涨至20万欧元。如果你在法国每年缴纳100万欧元的所得税，意大利无疑极具吸引力。至于美国公民，美国人总是要对全球收入纳税，因此移居意大利并不能减轻他们的税负。即使按30万欧元计算，对于年收入超过100万欧元的任何人来说，意大利的固定税率与欧洲其他任何地方相比仍然较低——彼得·费里尼奥·罗伯特告诉我，他有两位富有的法国朋友在过去几个月里移居意大利，但他们是从英国移居过去的。两人曾在伦敦金融城从事金融工作，他们渴望搬到一个财政制度像英国在改变针对富裕外国居民的规定之前那样对他们有利的地方。财富迁移专家Henley & Partners的税务服务总监彼得·费里尼奥表示：“即使按30万欧元计算，意大利的固定税率对于年收入超过100万欧元的任何人来说，与欧洲其他任何地方相比仍然较低。这意味着你可以在欧洲中心地带获得税收确定性和清晰度，而不必远走他乡。”巴黎税务律师杰罗姆·巴尔表示：“我们每周都会与想离开法国的人会面。他们对当前的税收状况感到不满，并担心未来税收会变得更加严苛。人们对政治气候缺乏信心。税收变化频繁，几乎每年都在变。人们担心在2027年新总统当选后，情况可能比现在更加艰难。”不过，杰罗姆·巴尔解释说，目前更多是“企业家和富人在考虑是否要移居，而不是真正付诸行动的人”。他强调：“移居需要全身心的投入和精心的规划。”他补充说，对于企业主而言，“他们需要改变公司的注册地。在法国，他们还需缴纳离境税。”如果许多法国富人正处于“考虑移居”的阶段，那么这个问题在阿拉伯联合酋长国则更为紧迫。彼得·费里尼奥表示，许多人重新考虑阿联酋是不可避免的。但对许多人来说，放弃迪拜的零税收制度将非常困难。巴尔说：“当你身处一个无需纳税的国家，再回到一个需要缴纳大量税款的国家是非常困难的。尤其是对于那些习惯了高消费的人来说，口袋里的净收入差异巨大。”他还补充说，习惯了零税收生活的人“不再习惯于行政手续——纳税申报、文件——所以这并不容易。”更多类似内容：• 迪拜旅游业遭受战争“残酷”冲击• 为何更多美国人现在移居爱尔兰• 纽约的大麻生意真的在腾飞吗

“许多人重新考虑阿联酋是不可避免的，”Henley & Partners的彼得·费里尼奥表示。“但我认为，当涉及工作、家庭等因素时，人们大规模连根拔起生活还为时过早。阿联酋的绝大多数人仍是从事普通工作的普通人，即使大多数百万富翁之所以成为百万富翁，是因为他们从事高薪工作，而非拥有资产。如果战争相对短暂，他们会留下。如果拖延下去，人们将不可避免地另寻他处，或将家庭迁走并远程工作，直到安全为止。如果你在阿联酋是为了工作，意大利不太可能有那么多同等职位，”他说。然而，中东战争很可能劝阻许多原本会移居阿联酋的富裕欧洲人。去年，根据Henley & Partners的数据，迪拜是百万富翁迁移的头号目的地，遥遥领先。这一数字在2026年必将大幅下降，而意大利凭借其对超级富豪的吸引力，以及其“甜蜜生活”的美誉，很可能成为受益者。——如需获取面向董事会及其他领域的全球洞察和专家分析，请订阅《商业世界》通讯，而《基本清单》则提供精选专题和见解。如需更多商业及相关内容，请在LinkedIn上关注我们。商业国际商业专题商业世界

readings.title: Can we afford Iran?
body: Today, Explained newsletter Can we afford Iran? As the war drags on, it risks eroding America’s ability to respond to other conflicts. by Caitlin Dewey Aug 31, 2026, 9:05 PM UTC Gift A Patriot missile is launched as part of the Patriot Air Defense System at White Sands Missile Range in New Mexico. Corbis via Getty Images Caitlin Dewey is a senior writer and editor at Vox, where she helms the Today, Explained newsletter. This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day. Subscribe here . President Donald Trump’s on-again, off-again war with Iran is officially on again. (So recursive is this never-ending conflict, in fact, that I had to search my inbox to confirm I hadn’t already written that sentence!) On Sunday, the US attacked rocket launchers Sunday on Iran’s Larak Island, claiming the strikes were necessary to prevent Iran from laying mines that could once again disrupt shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Iran, meanwhile, responded by firing a volley of ballistic missiles at US sites in the United Arab Emirates and Jordan, where they were reportedly intercepted. Email (required) Sign Up By submitting your email, you agree to our Terms and Privacy Notice . This site is protected by reCAPTCHA and the Google Privacy Policy and Terms of Service apply. The latest skirmish comes after a month of relative peace and quiet, and six months after the war began. You’ll recall that Trump initially said it would last four to five weeks at the very longest. But in the grand scheme of Trump’s Iran fictions, that optimistic timeline isn’t even the most flagrant. On Sunday night, the president also posted a video that purportedly showed Kharg Island, a central hub of Iran’s oil industry, “being blown to smithereens!!!” The video was, in fact, AI-generated . The persistence of the war in Iran isn’t merely exhausting for those of us following along at home. As a group of high-ranking military commanders recently warned the Pentagon, the drawn-out conflict could also make America less safe by limiting the military’s ability to respond to threats in other parts of the world. That unusual warning — first reported over the weekend by the Washington Post — suggested that the war in Iran is tying up ships and surveillance planes that the US needs elsewhere. Several top military leaders explicitly warned that the war had forced them to give up resources they needed to protect the US itself. That’s not the only risk of the ongoing conflict, either. Longer deployments have also eroded troop morale and disrupted ship maintenance . And as the war drags on, the US is burning through its stockpiles of advanced missiles , at a cost of many billions of dollars. None of this means we’re defenseless, of course. But the war in Iran is taking up a lot of bandwidth. And should another conflict break out anywhere else on earth…the US and its allies could feel it. One general warned the Pentagon that, without more resources, he could be forced to choose between protecting Israel and the US from ballistic missile attacks. And the Navy just moved its only dedicated aircraft carrier in the Pacific to the waters near Iran. “We are really robbing Peter to pay Paul,” one military expert told Vox in late February, even before we had any idea how long the war would last. ➨ Ditch the doorbell camera. More than 62 percent of respondents in a recent US News survey said they had an outdoor security camera at home. But there’s not much evidence that those cameras reduce crime — and they can damage your relationship with your neighbors . Did you know …that the known world basically ended around 1200 BCE ? A number of sophisticated civilizations collapsed at the same time, probably due to some combination of prolonged drought, earthquakes, migration, war and political instability. Today’s trivia: What was the name of Japan’s capital city before it was renamed Tokyo? (You can find this and other brain puzzles in Vox’s daily crossword . Look for the answer in tomorrow’s edition.) Yesterday’s trivia: Last week we asked you for the name of the athletic conference where Georgia Tech competes. That would be the ACC, or Atlantic Coast Conference, which confusingly includes a number of schools in the West and Midwest. ##段落

《今日解说》通讯：我们负担得起伊朗吗？随着战争拖延，它可能削弱美国应对其他冲突的能力。作者：凯特琳·杜威，2026年8月31日，晚上9:05 UTC 礼品 一枚爱国者导弹作为爱国者防空系统的一部分在新墨西哥州白沙导弹靶场发射。Corbis via Getty Images 凯特琳·杜威是Vox的高级撰稿人和编辑，负责《今日解说》通讯。本文发表于《今日解说》，这是一份每日通讯，帮助你理解当天最引人注目的新闻和故事。在此订阅。

##段落

唐纳德·特朗普总统与伊朗之间时断时续的战争正式再次打响。（事实上，这场无休止的冲突如此反复，以至于我不得不翻查收件箱来确认自己没有写过这句话！）周日，美国袭击了伊朗拉拉克岛上的火箭发射器，声称这些打击是必要的，以防止伊朗布设水雷，从而再次扰乱霍尔木兹海峡的航运。与此同时，伊朗向美国在阿联酋和约旦的基地发射了一连串弹道导弹，据报这些导弹已被拦截。电子邮件（必填） 注册 提交您的电子邮件即表示您同意我们的条款和隐私声明。本网站受reCAPTCHA保护，并适用Google隐私政策和服务条款。

##段落

最新这次小规模冲突发生在一个相对平静的月份之后，也是战争爆发六个月之后。您还记得，特朗普最初表示战争最多只会持续四到五周。但在特朗普关于伊朗的虚构叙事的宏大框架中，这个乐观的时间表甚至不是最离谱的。周日晚上，总统还发布了一段视频，据称显示伊朗石油工业的核心枢纽哈尔克岛“被炸成碎片！！！”事实上，该视频是人工智能生成的。

##段落

伊朗战争的持续不仅让国内关注此事的人们感到疲惫。正如一群高级军事指挥官最近向五角大楼警告的那样，这场拖延的冲突还可能限制军队应对世界其他地区威胁的能力，从而使美国变得更不安全。这一不同寻常的警告——最早在上周末由《华盛顿邮报》报道——表明伊朗战争正在牵制美国在其他地方所需的舰船和侦察机。几位高级军事领导人明确警告说，这场战争迫使他们放弃保护美国自身所需的资源。

##段落

这也不是持续冲突带来的唯一风险。更长的部署时间也削弱了部队士气，并扰乱了舰船维护。随着战争拖延，美国正在消耗其先进导弹的储备，成本高达数十亿美元。这些都不意味着我们毫无防御能力。

readings.title: Let’s stop calling them “soft skills” — and call them “real skills” instead
body: Let’s stop calling them “soft skills” — and call them “real skills” instead
We persist in hiring and training as if we’re running a bowling squad, as if easily measured skills are all that matter.

What causes successful organizations to fail ? What makes stocks fade, innovations slow, customers jump ship? We can agree that certain skills are essential. That hiring coders who can’t code, salespeople who can’t sell, or architects who can’t design is a waste. But these skills — let’s call them vocational skills — have become the backbone of the recruitment process.

But how do you explain that similar organizations, with similarly vocationally skilled people, find themselves with very different outcomes? Most of the textbooks that students experience and the tests they take are about vocational skills, the checkboxes that have to be checked to get a job. By misdefining “vocational” and focusing on these allegedly essential skills, we’ve diminished the value of the other skills that matter.

We give too little respect to the other skills when we call them “soft” and imply that they’re optional. What actually separates thriving organizations from struggling ones are the difficult-to-measure attitudes, processes and perceptions of the people who do the work.

Vocational skills can be taught: You’re not born knowing engineering or copywriting or even graphic design, therefore they must be something we can teach. But we let ourselves off the hook when it comes to decision-making, eager participation, dancing with fear, speaking with authority, working in teams , seeing the truth, speaking the truth, inspiring others, doing more than we’re asked, caring and being willing to change things. We underinvest in this training, fearful that these things are innate and can’t be taught. Perhaps they’re talents. And so we downplay them, calling them soft skills, making it easy for us to move on to something seemingly more urgent.

At scale, organizations pay less attention to soft skills when hiring because we’ve persuaded ourselves that vocational skills are impersonal and easier to measure. If it’s easier to test for, it seems more important when selecting our team.
And we fire slowly (and retrain rarely) when these skills are missing, because we’re worried about stepping on toes, being called out for getting personal or possibly wasting time on a lost cause.

But these skills can all be learned, as obvious skills like chess or typing can be learned. We learn them accidentally, by osmosis, by the collisions we have with teachers, parents, bosses and the world. Even though they’re more difficult to measure, that doesn’t mean we can’t improve them, can’t practice them or can’t change the way we do our work.

Let’s stop calling them soft. They’re interpersonal skills. Leadership skills. The skills of charisma and diligence and contribution. But these modifiers, while accurate, somehow edge them away from the vocational skills, the skills that we actually hire for, the skills we measure a graduate degree on.
So let’s uncomfortably call them real skills instead.
Real because they work, because they’re at the heart of what we need today.
Real because even if you’ve got the vocational skills, you’re no help to us without these human skills, the things that we can’t write down or program a computer to do.
Real skills can’t replace vocational skills, of course. What they can do is amplify the things you’ve already been measuring.
Imagine a team member with all the traditional vocational skills: productive, skilled, experienced. A resume that can prove it. That’s a fine baseline.

Now add to it. Perceptive, charismatic, driven, focused, goal-setting, inspiring and motivated. Generous, empathic and consistent. A deep listener , with patience. What happens to your organization when someone like that joins your team?
Writing in the Harvard Business Review , Lou Solomon reports that 69 percent of managers are uncomfortable communicating with their employees. I’d guess that many of the other 31 percent are lying.

Communicating with employees is uncomfortable because we’ve built systems of compliance and dominance that make it difficult. We ask people to leave their humanity at the door, then use authority to change behavior. We overlay corporate greed and short-term thinking with a human desire to create work that matters.

How do we build people-centric organizations while also accepting the fact that two thirds of our managers (presumably well paid, well trained and integral to our success) are so uncomfortable doing an essential part of their job that they admitted it to a stranger?

In a recent survey, the Graduate Management Admission Council reported that although MBAs were strong in analytical aptitude, quantitative expertise and information-gathering ability, they were sorely lacking in other critical areas that employers find equally attractive: strategic thinking, written and oral communication, leadership and adaptability . Are these mutually exclusive? Must we trade one for the other?

The foundation of all real skills is this one: the confidence and permission to talk to one another. Not to manage, belittle, intimidate or control. Simply to seek to be understood and to do the work to understand.

##段落
让我们别再称它们为“软技能”——改叫“真技能”吧  
2023年6月9日  
/  
赛斯·戈丁  
Facebook  
X  
LinkedIn  
Reddit  
WhatsApp  
黛博拉·斯皮尔曼  
我们仍然像经营保龄球队一样招聘和培训，仿佛只有那些容易衡量的技能才重要。

##段落
是什么导致成功组织走向失败？是什么让股票下跌、创新放缓、客户流失？我们都能认同某些技能是必不可少的。招聘不会写代码的程序员、不会销售的销售员或不会设计的建筑师，纯属浪费。但这些技能——让我们称它们为“职业技能”——已成为招聘流程的支柱。

##段落
但你怎么解释，拥有同样职业技能的相似组织，却往往结果迥异？学生们接触的大多数教科书和参加的考试，都聚焦于职业技能，即那些为了获得工作而必须勾选的条条框框。通过错误定义“职业”并专注于这些所谓的关键技能，我们贬低了其他重要技能的价值。

##段落
当我们称其他技能为“软”技能，暗示它们是可有可无的，我们就对它们尊重不足。真正区分繁荣组织与挣扎组织的，是那些难以衡量的态度、流程和从业者的认知。

##段落
职业技能可以被传授：你并非天生就懂工程、文案或平面设计，因此它们必定是可以教的东西。但在决策、积极参与、与恐惧共舞、有权威地表达、团队合作、看清真相、说出真相、激励他人、超越要求地付出、关心他人以及愿意改变这些事情上，我们却让自己逃脱了责任。我们在这方面的培训投入不足，担心这些东西是天生的、无法传授的。或许它们是天赋。于是我们轻描淡写，称它们为软技能，让我们轻易转向看似更紧迫的事情。

##段落
在规模层面，组织在招聘时对软技能的关注较少，因为我们说服自己职业技能是非个人的、更容易衡量。如果更容易测试，它似乎在选团队时就更重要。

##段落
而当这些技能缺失时，我们解雇缓慢（且很少再培训），因为我们担心踩到别人的脚趾、被指责过于个人化，或可能在无望的事情上浪费时间。

##段落
但这些技能全都可以学会，就像下棋或打字这类显而易见的技能可以学会一样。我们是通过偶然、耳濡目染、通过与老师、父母、老板和世界的碰撞而学会它们的。即使它们更难衡量，那也不意味着我们无法改进、无法练习。

我们无法改变工作方式吗？  
当然可以。  
别再称它们为“软技能”了。它们是人际技能，是领导技能，是魅力、勤奋和贡献的技能。但这些修饰词虽然准确，却不知何故将它们与职业技能、我们实际招聘时看重的技能、我们衡量研究生学位的技能拉开了距离。  
所以，让我们不自在地称它们为“真实技能”。  
真实，因为它们有效，因为它们是我们今天所需的核心。  
真实，因为即使你拥有职业技能，没有这些人类技能——那些我们无法写下来或编程让计算机去做的事情——你对我们毫无帮助。  
真实技能当然不能取代职业技能。它们能做的是放大你已经在衡量的东西。  
想象一个拥有所有传统职业技能的团队成员：高效、熟练、经验丰富，简历可以证明这一切。那是一个不错的基线。  
现在再加上：敏锐、有魅力、有驱动力、专注、目标明确、鼓舞人心且积极主动。慷慨、富有同理心且始终如一。耐心倾听，深入理解。当这样一个人加入你的团队时，你的组织会发生什么变化？  
在《哈佛商业评论》中，卢·所罗门报道，69%的管理者与员工沟通时感到不适。我猜其他31%中许多人是在撒谎。  
与员工沟通之所以不适，是因为我们建立了顺从和支配的系统，使沟通变得困难。我们要求人们把人性留在门外，然后用权威来改变行为。我们将企业贪婪和短期思维与创造有意义工作的渴望叠加在一起。  
我们如何建立以人为本的组织，同时接受这样一个事实：我们三分之二的管理者（想必薪酬优厚、训练有素且对我们的成功至关重要）在做一项基本工作时如此不适，以至于向陌生人承认了这一点？  
在最近的一项调查中，研究生入学管理委员会报告称，尽管MBA在分析能力、量化专长和信息收集能力方面很强，但他们在雇主同样看重的其他关键领域严重欠缺：战略思维、书面和口头沟通、领导力和适应性。这些是相互排斥的吗？我们必须牺牲一个来换取另一个吗？  
所有真实技能的基础是这一点：拥有彼此交谈的自信和许可。不是去管理、贬低、恐吓或控制。只是寻求被理解，并努力去理解。  
摘自赛斯·高汀的《意义之歌：团队新宣言》，经企鹅兰登书屋旗下投资组合出版社同意转载。

readings.title: How social media ceased to be social
body: 22 May 2026 Share Save Add as preferred on Google John Laurenson Social media platforms used to be about communication between friends – now many are increasingly short video entertainment hubs. The business model is to increase the time people spend on their apps and increase ad revenue. But is there already a consumer backlash? Aurélia fixes herself a coffee, sits down in her beautiful garden not far from Paris and goes on Instagram "to relax." First up: "a guy I like a lot who does interior design. He's in Venice at the moment." She's into interior design, and has even just had two bird drawings by the 19th Century English designer William Morris tattooed on her arms. She scrolls down. Two kittens having a fight. "I love animals so I get a lot of animals. That's how it works, social media. You click on bananas and they give you bananas." There are ads too – although they look just like the other posts – for a robot-vacuum cleaner, a diet and bed linen (with Morris-inspired designs). But no friends. She has 198 on Instagram but she says "it's completely changed. I practically don’t see any friends' posts anymore." She’s pretty much given up posting herself. "I don't think anyone sees them anymore anyway."  While there remain committed social, amateur posters on Instagram and especially Facebook, the switch from communicating with people you know to scrolling through professionally made content from people you don't, is even more pronounced among young users. Kylian, 16, is in vocational training to become a chef. He's on TikTok and Youtube a lot, he says. "I like looking at videos more than photos or messages. I watch videos made by people I don't know. I don’t post at all. I'm a rather shy person. I stay in my bubble. I watch and that’s all. I keep my reactions to myself." "I spend a lot of time scrolling through videos made by content-creators," says Lucie, also 16. "They're more interesting than the posts of people I know." She doesn't post except sometimes "stories" which disappear after 24 hours.  Whether it's TikTok, Snapchat, Facebook and Instagram, we are a long way from the "digital town square" of personal interaction that social media was even just a few years ago. In France, annual official Barometre du numerique 2026  shows 49% of social media users are "active only occasionally". In the UK, an Ofcom report   published in April showed a year-on-year drop of users who actively post from 61% to 49%. In the US, a Morning Consult survey of June last year found 28% reported posting less often than the previous year. Just 33% now post daily compared to 57% who use it for entertainment daily. The gap is a lot wider still for Gen Z – 18% active for 74% passive. Vanessa Lalo, a Paris-based clinical psychologist specialising in on-line behaviour, says "users have become more conscious that the traces you leave (on social media) stay there forever and some no longer want to maintain social media relations that can be superficial. Some don’t want the exposure to criticism that might be a risk when you post or the feeling that their post will seem poor alongside all the professional content". However, Lalo adds, people haven’t stopped posting, rather they are posting different things and in different places. "On TikTok, for example, young people publish a lot of content but it's more funny parodies and remixes of existing material. The goal is to make people laugh, not to tell people about their lives." That still happens, she says, but it’s moved from social media platforms like Instagram and Facebook to messaging sites like WhatsApp. There's also been a move towards private groups on Instagram and Snapchat. "These are much more intimate places where you're not bombarded with ads and content made by influencers," she says. "What we're seeing is social media splitting in two," says social media consultant Matt Navarra, author of the Geekout Newsletter. "Big platforms like Instagram and TikTok are becoming more about entertainment and discovery. WhatsApp is becoming the place people go to actually be social. The catch is, those kinds of spaces are harder for companies to make money from." Small business owners are being pushed to become presenters, editors, trend spotters and content creators, on top of actually running the business – Matt Navarra It was TikTok that helped to pioneer an algorithm that figures out from the moment you start scrolling what you like, and then fills your feed with material calculated to keep you on the app for the longest possible time. Now, says Matt Navarra, "Meta has built what it calls an AI system for unconnected content recommendations on Facebook and Instagram, which basically means, they're increasingly showing you stuff from people you don't follow because the machine thinks you're going to like it. It's not biased towards, is it a professional creator? Is it a brand? Is it a friend? If they can see that you've engaged with a friend a lot, you might see a lot more of their content. It's just that who you are friends with, who you follow, has become irrelevant in a way." This all means that small businesses, that have long used social media for free promotion have to up their game.   "There's a real opportunity for some small businesses," says Matt Navarra. "A bakery, florist, salon or local café can still break through if they have a good story, strong visuals or behind-the-scenes content people want to watch. But it also means the job has changed. Small business owners are being pushed to become presenters, editors, trend spotters and content creators, on top of actually running the business." The social platforms continue to be monetised predominantly by ad revenue. That is still the core business model. And ad revenue continues to grow – Matt Navarra Social media is evolving into something passive like television, albeit television that adapts as you zap. Or rather which knows you so well that it doesn't seem to matter that much that it's taken the remote control. You give the platform information about yourself that it uses for commercial gain and, in return, it gives you content tailored to please you for free. The transition from truly social media to entertainment platform does seem to be paying off. "The social platforms continue to be monetised predominantly by ad revenue. That is still the core business model. And ad revenue continues to grow," says Matt Navarra. Global social media ad revenue is expected to reach $317 billion (£236bn) in 2026, up from $277 billion (£206bn) last year. Meta is the biggest winner. Its ad sales already increased 22% year-on-year in 2025.  Ad sales are expected to hit $243 billion (£181bn) this year , enough to overtake Google for the first time. AI powered digital ad targeting is becoming ever more effective and precise. "The social platforms allow companies to put ads amongst the content that you're scrolling through. Every third or fourth scroll is an ad. And they are the world's best ad targeting engines. They know so much about your interests because of what you've looked at, liked, engaged with, what you've chosen to follow, the time you've spent in certain areas of the app, things like that," Navarra says.  "So advertisers will go in and say: 'I want to place an ad next to people in the UK who are between thirty and sixty years old and who are interested in DIY' and the social platforms will have that information and will place the ads accordingly." The price will depend on the number of impressions (clicks) the advertiser wants and how tight the criteria are. It costs more to place ads in the social media feeds of people who buy horses than people who buy ice-cream. More like this: •  TikTok is tracking you, even if you don't use the app. Here's how to stop it •  How to stop AI from turning your brain to mush •  This monkey selfie will protect you from AI slop Might there be a backlash coming? Don't many people go on to social media to see how friends are reacting to their posts or comments before settling down to scroll through professionally made content? Whether it's the shrinking social motivation to get on these apps or something else, the amount of time people spend on social media plateaued at an average of 141 minutes in 2025, down slightly from 143 minutes in 2024 . However, this is only part of the story, as the number of people using social media and the total time humanity spends on these apps continues to rise. For Gen Z it’s higher still. Around five hours a day in the United States where, for this demographic, social media has also become the primary search engine and shopping tool. Meanwhile, for those who miss what are fast becoming the old days when social media enabled you to share a bit of your life, a joke or a point of view with people you more-or-less knew, there are tools within platforms, says Matt Navarra, that allow you to choose to see mainly friends and family content. "People can flick to a feed that gives them that," he says. "But most people don't." -- If you liked this story, sign up for The Essential List newsletter – a handpicked selection of features, videos and can't-miss news, delivered to your inbox twice a week.   For more on business and beyond, follow us on  LinkedIn . 社交媒体平台曾经用于朋友间的交流——如今许多平台日益成为短视频娱乐中心。其商业模式是增加人们在应用上花费的时间，并提高广告收入。但消费者是否已经出现反弹？

##段落

奥蕾莉亚给自己冲了一杯咖啡，坐在巴黎附近美丽的花园里，打开Instagram“放松一下”。首先映入眼帘的是：“一个我非常喜欢的做室内设计的家伙。他现在在威尼斯。”她对室内设计情有独钟，甚至刚刚把19世纪英国设计师威廉·莫里斯的两幅鸟类画纹在了手臂上。她往下滑动。两只小猫在打架。“我喜欢动物，所以会刷到很多动物内容。社交媒体就是这样运作的。你点击香蕉，它就给你推送香蕉。”还有广告——尽管看起来和其他帖子没什么两样——涉及扫地机器人、减肥餐和床品（带有莫里斯风格的设计）。但看不到朋友。她在Instagram上有198个好友，但她说“情况完全变了。我几乎再也看不到任何朋友的帖子了。”她自己也基本不再发帖了。“我觉得反正也没人会看。”

##段落

虽然在Instagram尤其是Facebook上仍有热衷社交的业余发帖者，但从与认识的人交流转向浏览陌生人的专业制作内容，这一趋势在年轻用户中尤为明显。16岁的基利安正在接受厨师职业培训。他说自己经常刷TikTok和YouTube。“我喜欢看视频胜过看照片或消息。我看的是不认识的人制作的视频。我完全不发帖。我是个比较害羞的人。我待在自己的小圈子里。只看不说话。我把反应藏在心里。”

##段落

“我花很多时间刷内容创作者制作的视频，”同样16岁的露西说。“它们比认识的人的帖子更有趣。”她除了偶尔发一些24小时后消失的“快拍”外，从不发帖。无论是TikTok、Snapchat、Facebook还是Instagram，我们早已远离了社交媒体几年前还是“数字城镇广场”式的个人互动时代。在法国，2026年官方年度《数字晴雨表》显示，49%的社交媒体用户“仅偶尔活跃”。在英国，4月发布的Ofcom报告显示，积极发帖的用户同比下降，从61%降至49%。在美国，去年6月Morning Consult的一项调查发现，28%的受访者表示发帖频率低于前一年。目前只有33%的人每天发帖，而每天使用社交媒体进行娱乐的人比例为57%。在Z世代中，这一差距更加悬殊——18%积极发帖，74%被动浏览。瓦内萨·拉洛，一位驻巴黎的临床心理学家，专攻在线行为研究。

她说：“用户已经越来越意识到，你在社交媒体上留下的痕迹会永远存在，有些人不再愿意维护可能肤浅的社交媒体关系。有些人不想暴露在发帖可能带来的批评风险中，或者担心自己的帖子在众多专业内容中显得逊色。”然而，拉洛补充说，人们并没有停止发帖，而是换了内容和地点。“例如，在TikTok上，年轻人发布大量内容，但更多是对现有素材的有趣模仿和混剪。目标是让人们发笑，而不是分享生活。”她说，分享生活仍然存在，但已从Instagram和Facebook等平台转移到WhatsApp等即时通讯应用。此外，人们也在转向Instagram和Snapchat上的私密群组。“这些是更私密的空间，你不会被广告和网红内容轰炸，”她说。

社交媒体顾问马特·纳瓦拉（Matt Navarra）在《极客通讯》（Geekout Newsletter）中写道：“我们看到社交媒体正在一分为二。像Instagram和TikTok这样的大平台越来越侧重于娱乐和发现。WhatsApp则成为人们真正社交的地方。问题是，这类空间更难让企业获利。”小型企业主被迫成为主持人、编辑、潮流观察者和内容创作者，同时还要实际经营业务——马特·纳瓦拉。

正是TikTok率先开创了一种算法，从你开始滚动屏幕的那一刻就能判断你喜欢什么，然后填充你的信息流，以计算出的内容让你在应用上停留尽可能长的时间。现在，马特·纳瓦拉说，“Meta已经在其Facebook和Instagram上构建了一个所谓的AI系统，用于非关联内容推荐，这基本上意味着，它们越来越倾向于向你展示你不关注的人的内容，因为机器认为你会喜欢。它不偏向于是否专业创作者、品牌或朋友。如果它看到你和某个朋友互动很多，你可能会看到更多他们的内容。只是，你的朋友是谁、你关注谁，在某种程度上已经变得无关紧要。”这一切意味着，长期利用社交媒体进行免费推广的小型企业必须提升自己的水平。

“对于一些小企业来说，确实存在机会，”马特·纳瓦拉说。“面包店、花店、沙龙或本地咖啡馆，如果有好故事、强视觉或人们想看的幕后内容，仍然可以脱颖而出。但这也意味着工作方式已经改变。小型企业主被迫成为主持人、编辑、潮流观察者和内容创作者，同时还要实际经营业务。”

##段落
真正经营业务的核心部分。"社交平台仍然主要通过广告收入实现商业化，这依然是核心商业模式，且广告收入持续增长——马特·纳瓦拉。社交媒体正演变为一种类似电视的被动媒介，尽管是那种会随着你切换频道而适应的电视，或者更确切地说，是一种对你如此了解，以至于它拿走遥控器这件事似乎也没那么重要的电视。你向平台提供关于自己的信息，平台利用这些信息获取商业利益，作为回报，它免费为你提供量身定制的取悦内容。从真正的社交媒体向娱乐平台的转变似乎确实在奏效。"社交平台仍然主要通过广告收入实现商业化，这依然是核心商业模式，且广告收入持续增长，"马特·纳瓦拉表示。全球社交媒体广告收入预计将从去年的2770亿美元（2060亿英镑）增长至2026年的3170亿美元（2360亿英镑）。Meta是最大的赢家，其2025年广告销售额已同比增长22%，预计今年将达到2430亿美元（1810亿英镑），足以首次超越谷歌。AI驱动的数字广告定向投放正变得前所未有的高效和精准。"社交平台允许企业在你浏览的内容中插入广告，每滚动三四次就会出现一条广告。它们是全球最优秀的广告定向引擎，因为你的浏览记录、点赞、互动、关注选择、在应用特定区域停留的时间等信息，它们对你的兴趣了如指掌，"纳瓦拉说。"因此广告主会说：'我想把广告投放给英国30至60岁、对DIY感兴趣的人群'，社交平台掌握这些信息，就会相应地进行广告投放。"价格取决于广告主想要的曝光次数（点击量）以及筛选条件的严格程度。将广告投放到购买马匹的人群的社交媒体信息流中，比投放到购买冰淇淋的人群要花费更多。

##段落
更多类似内容：• TikTok正在追踪你，即使你不使用该应用，以下是阻止方法 • 如何防止AI让你的大脑变得迟钝 • 这张猴子自拍照将保护你免受AI垃圾内容的侵害

##段落
是否会有反弹出现？难道不是很多人先上社交媒体看看朋友对自己的帖子或评论有何反应，然后才安下心来浏览专业制作的内容吗？无论是使用这些应用的社交动力减弱还是其他原因，人们在社交媒体上花费的时间在2025年趋于平稳，平均为141分钟，略低于2024年的143分钟。然而，这只是故事的一部分，因为使用社交媒体的人数

##段落  
人工智能以及人类在这些应用上花费的总时间持续增长。对于Z世代而言，这一数字更高。在美国，这一群体每天约花费五小时，社交媒体已成为他们的主要搜索引擎和购物工具。与此同时，对于那些怀念社交媒体刚兴起时、能与熟人分享生活点滴、笑话或观点的人，平台内也有工具可选，马特·纳瓦拉表示，用户可以选择主要查看朋友和家人的内容。他说：“人们可以切换到那种信息流，但大多数人并不这么做。”——如果你喜欢这个故事，请订阅《必读清单》新闻通讯，每周两次精选专题、视频和不可错过的新闻，直接发送到你的邮箱。如需更多商业及其他领域内容，请在领英上关注我们。商业科技专题社交媒体商业世界

readings.title: The bears cooling off in a California pool
body: 3 days ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Isabelle Gerretsen Black bears love lounging in Brian Gordon and Ricardo Martinez's pool in Los Angeles. As bear encounters increase across Southern California, the couple share videos of their furry visitors and reveal how they are co-existing with these wild animals. When Brian Gordon first learned that black bears were swimming in the pool of the house he was buying in Los Angeles, he was very afraid. "I'd never seen a bear in real life. I said, 'We'll just build a big wall with barbed wire,'" he recalls. Four years later, Gordon loves nothing more than seeing a family of bears playing in his pool and running around his garden. The furry visitors stop by several times a week. (Scroll down to watch a video of the bears at play.) "They are fine to come here and scratch on the trees, take a nap, and jump in the pool if it's hot, as long as we're not creating harm for them, or for ourselves," Gordon says. Gordon and his partner Ricardo Martinez have made it their mission to peacefully share their pool and garden with the bears. But behind these charming videos of bears relaxing in their pool, there's a deeper story of vigilance and safety precautions that make this co-existence possible. The couple live in Monrovia, Los Angeles County, in Southern California, home to around 1,600 bears . Their house is in the foothills of the San Gabriel Mountains and borders the Angeles National Forest, which spans 700,000 acres (2,830sq km). When the couple moved in, they started spotting bears almost immediately. They initially tried to chase the bears away by yelling, using air horns and occasionally a paintball gun with soft rubber pellets. "But it felt horrible," says Martinez. "It did not sit right with us. We said that as long as they're not breaking into the home and getting into the trash, then they're ok to come by." They sought an approach that would keep both themselves and the bears safe, despite close proximity. "We've since settled on less aggressive means, and honestly, they work better for us," says Gordon. We have had bears crashing barbecues – Brian Gordon Martinez says that black bears are "misunderstood". "They are not going to eat you," says Martinez. Black bear attacks are incredibly rare, with just one fatal attack recorded in California's history .  The couple say they always keep a "healthy distance" from the bears and stay inside when the animals are around. There are sometimes unplanned encounters though.  "We have had bears crashing barbecues," says Gordon. "But if they see you, they usually just walk away." Gordon and Martinez say their favourite bear visitor is Maddie, who they first got to know as an incredibly inquisitive youngster in 2023. She loved playing in the pool and hanging around the garden. "She is our golden child," says Martinez. A year later, Maddie returned with her cubs in tow. "Unfortunately she lost those cubs, so we went through an emotional rollercoaster with her," says Martinez. This year she has brought her new cubs to the house. "They're the most adorable [creatures] you've ever seen. They're so cuddly but also intimidating, with their long claws." We live here and the bears live here. We don't want them to go anywhere – Ricardo Martinez Punky is another "rambunctious yearling" who first came to the house as a cub with her mother, says Gordon. "She would pop all the pool floaties." She once climbed onto an inflatable cupcake and drifted into the middle of the pool. "She really stole our hearts that summer with her pool fun," says Gordon. They nicknamed another regular visitor "Nappy", as the female bear likes to take long siestas while floating in the pool. "She'll literally go to the steps of the pool, get in and put her head down. She's the only bear I've seen take hour-long naps in the pool," says Gordon. If she sees the couple, Nappy will huff at them. "She's a big mama bear and she's just a little grumpy about everything in life," Gordon jokes. These characters are among a growing number of black bears trying to make a home alongside Californians , and often posing challenges for local communities.  There are more than 60,000 black bears living in California , says Wilson Sherman, a research fellow at the University of California, Los Angeles. Black bears are an increasingly common sight in LA suburbs. "They are really intelligent, adaptable omnivores. They eat everything and have learned how to gain calories in places where people live," says Sherman, who studies how communities respond to black bears.  Not all bear encounters are as positive as Gordon and Martinez's experience though. "We do see incidents pretty regularly of bears raiding trash and entering homes," says Sherman. "The really sad thing about this is that when things go awry, it's usually the bears that end up paying the price. Several bears have been put down in the last few years.   A mother black bear called Blondie was euthanised by the California Department of Fish and Wildlife in March 2026 after she swiped at a woman walking her dog in Monrovia.  Blondie had also visited Gordon and Martinez's garden a few times and never caused any problems. Gordon organised a petition to try to prevent the euthanasia, which was signed by almost 6,000 people. "It was pretty devastating. Blondie resembles all mama bears, just trying to find shelter, to raise her kids and live her life," he says. The California Department of Fish and Wildlife says that DNA testing revealed that the captured bear was responsible for the incident, as well as a previous attack on an elderly resident sitting on his porch in Monrovia in June 2025. "Euthanasia is used only as a last resort when an animal poses a risk to public safety and cannot be safely returned to the wild," says a spokesperson. "Relocation may seem like a solution but is not an option when it could put public safety at risk. Bears have strong spatial memory and often return to familiar areas." The bear's cubs are being cared for at a wildlife rehabilitation centre and will be released into a suitable habitat when they are ready, he adds. To minimise conflict with bears, Sherman says it is important that communities restrict access to attractants, such as rubbish bins and leaving food outdoors.  "For a bear, finding a box that's full of pizza when you've been spending your time digging for worms and roots is a game changer." Keeping neighbourhoods bear-free is a "collective training effort", Sherman adds. "You all have to be on the same page, because if one person's leaving a lot of really good stuff in their yard, the bear is very likely going to think, 'I should check out a handful of other yards.'" Gordon says that they are "hypervigilant" when it comes to waste. "We don't even use our trash cans. I haul it to my office, a couple of times a week." They also keep their doors and windows closed and don't ever leave food in their car. They're not teddy bears, they are still wild animals – Wilson Sherman The couple say they have never had a negative encounter with any of the bears visiting their home. Martinez once found Nappy in the garage when he'd accidentally left it open. "We both startled each other," he says. "I slowly walked back, because you don't ever want to corner a bear." She emerged from the garage and went on her way, he says. More like this:
Why grizzly bears need their own hiking trails
The true story of Germany ' s rampant raccoons

Social media accounts, like Martinez and Gordon's, and home surveillance cameras are allowing people "to understand bears as individuals and providing an intimate look into their lives", says Sherman. But he has some reservations. "There's always the risk of Disneyfication, of painting too fuzzy a picture. They're not teddy bears, they are still wild animals." Sherman warns that it is important that bears and humans don't become too comfortable around each other. "Part of loving bears is creating healthy boundaries and setting the bears up for success when they inevitably pass through our neighbourhoods," he says. Through their Instagram account dedicated to the bears, @poolbearlife, Gordon and Martinez hope to raise awareness of how people can behave safely around bears and how to mitigate unwanted encounters. They stress that their relationship with black bears is not something that could necessarily be universal. "This works for us, for where we live," says Gordon.  "It's all about finding that balance with wildlife, how can we co-thrive?" says Martinez. "We live here and the bears live here. We don't want them to go anywhere." -- For essential climate news and hopeful developments to your inbox, sign up to the  Future Earth newsletter, while  The Essential List delivers a handpicked selection of features and insights twice a week.   For more science, technology, environment and health stories from the BBC, follow us on  Facebook and  Instagram . ##段落
三天前 分享 保存 设为Google首选 伊莎贝尔·杰勒特森 黑熊喜欢在洛杉矶布莱恩·戈登和里卡多·马丁内斯的泳池里消遣。随着南加州熊出没事件日益增多，这对夫妇分享了他们毛茸茸访客的视频，并透露了他们如何与这些野生动物共存。

##段落
当布莱恩·戈登第一次得知黑熊在他正打算购买的洛杉矶房子里游泳时，他非常害怕。“我从未在现实生活中见过熊。我说，‘我们干脆建一堵带铁丝网的高墙吧，’”他回忆道。四年后，戈登最爱的莫过于看着一家熊在他的泳池里玩耍、在花园里跑来跑去。这些毛茸茸的访客每周都会光顾好几次。（向下滚动观看熊玩耍的视频。）“它们来这里抓抓树、打个盹、天热了跳进泳池，完全没问题，只要我们不伤害它们，也不伤害我们自己，”戈登说。

##段落
戈登和他的伴侣里卡多·马丁内斯把与熊和平共享泳池和花园视为自己的使命。但在这些熊在泳池中放松的迷人视频背后，是一个关于警惕和安全防范的更深层故事，正是这些让共存成为可能。

##段落
这对夫妇住在南加州洛杉矶县蒙罗维亚，那里是大约1600只熊的家园。他们的房子位于圣盖博山脉山麓，紧邻占地70万英亩（2830平方公里）的安吉利斯国家森林。夫妇俩搬进来后，几乎立刻就发现了熊的踪迹。他们起初试图通过大喊大叫、使用气喇叭，偶尔用装有软橡胶弹丸的彩弹枪来驱赶熊。“但那感觉糟透了，”马丁内斯说。“我们心里过意不去。我们说，只要它们不闯进屋里、不翻垃圾桶，那它们来转转就没问题。”他们寻求一种既能保证自身安全又能保护熊的方法，尽管彼此距离很近。“我们后来采用了不那么激进的手段，老实说，这对我们更有效，”戈登说。

##段落
我们遇到过熊闯入烧烤现场的情况——布莱恩·戈登 马丁内斯说黑熊“被误解了”。“它们不会吃掉你的，”马丁内斯说。黑熊袭击事件极为罕见，加州历史上仅记录过一例致命袭击。这对夫妇表示，他们始终与熊保持“安全距离”，当动物在附近时，他们就待在室内。不过有时也会发生意外相遇。“我们遇到过熊闯入烧烤现场的情况，”戈登说。“但如果它们看到你，通常只会走开。”戈登和马丁内斯说，他们最喜欢的熊访客是麦迪，他们最初在2023年认识她时，她还是一只极其好奇的小熊。她喜欢在泳池里玩耍，喜欢在周围闲逛。

##段落
“她是我们的金孩子，”马丁内斯说。一年后，玛蒂带着她的幼崽回来了。“不幸的是，她失去了那些幼崽，所以我们和她一起经历了情绪上的过山车，”马丁内斯说。今年，她带着新生的幼崽来到了房子。“它们是你见过的最可爱的[生物]。它们非常惹人喜爱，但也令人畏惧，因为它们有长长的爪子。”我们住在这里，熊也住在这里。我们不想让它们去任何地方——里卡多·马丁内斯

##段落
Punky是另一只“精力充沛的一岁熊”，戈登说，她最初是作为幼崽和母亲一起来到房子的。“她会把所有的泳池浮具都弄破。”她曾经爬上一个充气蛋糕，漂到泳池中央。“那个夏天，她在泳池里的乐趣真的俘获了我们的心，”戈登说。他们给另一位常客起了个绰号叫“纳皮”，因为这只母熊喜欢在泳池里漂浮时打长长的午盹。“她真的会走到泳池台阶边，进去，把头低下。她是我见过的唯一一只在泳池里打一小时盹的熊，”戈登说。如果她看到这对夫妇，纳皮会朝他们喷气。“她是个熊妈妈，对生活中的一切都有点暴躁，”戈登开玩笑说。

##段落
这些角色是越来越多的黑熊试图与加州人共同安家的一部分，它们经常给当地社区带来挑战。加州大学洛杉矶分校的研究员威尔逊·谢尔曼说，加州生活着超过6万只黑熊。黑熊在洛杉矶郊区越来越常见。“它们是非常聪明、适应性强的杂食动物。它们什么都吃，并且学会了如何在人类居住的地方获取卡路里，”研究社区如何应对黑熊的谢尔曼说。

##段落
并非所有与熊的相遇都像戈登和马丁内斯的经历那样积极。“我们确实经常看到熊翻垃圾和闯入房屋的事件，”谢尔曼说。“真正可悲的是，当事情出错时，通常最终付出代价的是熊。过去几年里，有几只熊被处死了。”一只名叫布隆迪的母黑熊在2026年3月于蒙罗维亚抓伤一名遛狗的女性后，被加州鱼类和野生动物部门实施安乐死。布隆迪也曾几次造访戈登和马丁内斯的花园，从未造成任何问题。戈登组织了一份请愿书，试图阻止安乐死，有近6000人签名。“这非常令人心碎。布隆迪和所有熊妈妈一样，只是在试图寻找庇护所，抚养孩子，过自己的生活，”他说。加州鱼类和野生动物部门表示，DNA测试证实，被捕获的熊对这起事件以及之前的一起事件负有责任。

2025年6月，蒙罗维亚一位年长居民坐在自家门廊时遭到袭击。“安乐死仅在动物对公共安全构成风险且无法安全放归野外时，作为最后手段使用，”一位发言人表示。“搬迁看似是解决方案，但当可能危及公共安全时，这并非选项。熊具有强烈的空间记忆，往往会返回熟悉的区域。”他补充说，这只熊的幼崽正在野生动物康复中心接受照料，待时机成熟后将放归适宜的栖息地。谢尔曼表示，为尽量减少与熊的冲突，社区限制接触诱因（如垃圾桶和户外遗留食物）至关重要。“对一只熊来说，当你一直在挖蠕虫和树根为食时，发现一个装满披萨的盒子简直是改变命运的事。”保持社区无熊是一项“集体训练努力”，谢尔曼补充道。“所有人都必须达成共识，因为如果一个人院子里留了大量好东西，熊很可能想，‘我应该去检查其他几个院子。’”戈登表示，他们在垃圾处理方面“高度警惕”。“我们甚至不用自家的垃圾桶。我每周几次把垃圾运到办公室。”他们还保持门窗关闭，并且从不将食物留在车内。它们不是泰迪熊，它们仍然是野生动物——威尔逊·谢尔曼这对夫妇表示，他们从未与到访家中的任何熊有过负面接触。马丁内斯曾有一次不小心让车库门开着，发现纳皮在里面。“我们互相吓了一跳，”他说。“我慢慢后退，因为你永远不想困住一只熊。”他说，她从车库出来，然后离开了。更多类似内容：
为什么灰熊需要自己的徒步小径
看到熊时该怎么办
德国浣熊泛滥的真实故事谢尔曼表示，像马丁内斯和戈登这样的社交媒体账号以及家庭监控摄像头，让人们“将熊视为个体，并得以亲密一窥它们的生活”。但他有些保留意见。“总有迪士尼化的风险，把画面描绘得过于温馨。它们不是泰迪熊，它们仍然是野生动物。”谢尔曼警告说，熊和人类彼此过于舒适相处是危险的。“爱熊的一部分在于建立健康的界限，并确保熊在不可避免地经过我们社区时能够顺利生存，”他说。通过他们专门记录熊的Instagram账号@poolbearlife，戈登和马丁内斯希望提高人们对如何在熊周围安全行为以及如何减少不必要遭遇的认识。他们强调，他们与黑熊的关系是

这未必是放之四海而皆准的做法。戈登说：“这对我们有效，适合我们生活的地方。”马丁内斯说：“关键在于找到与野生动物共存的平衡点，我们如何共同繁荣？”“我们住在这里，熊也住在这里。我们不希望它们去任何地方。”——如需获取关键气候新闻和有希望的进展，请订阅《未来地球》简报，而《要闻清单》每周两次为您精选专题和见解。欲了解更多BBC科学、技术、环境和健康报道，请在Facebook和Instagram上关注我们。地球 野生动物 自然与户外 环境 热浪 专题 熊

readings.title: The Supreme Court just gave Trump his illegal ballroom
body: Politics The Supreme Court just gave Trump his illegal ballroom And the justices didn’t even bother to explain why… by Ian Millhiser Aug 31, 2026, 9:45 PM UTC Gift President Donald Trump talks to reporters on May 19, 2026 about his proposed White House ballroom next to what used to be the East Wing. Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images Ian Millhiser is a senior correspondent at Vox, where he focuses on the Supreme Court, the Constitution, and the decline of liberal democracy in the United States. He received a JD from Duke University and is the author of two books on the Supreme Court. Welp, the Supreme Court has decided that President Donald Trump gets to build his ballroom. The decision in National Park Service v. National Trust for Historic Preservation is 5-4, with Republican Chief Justice John Roberts joining the three Democratic justices in dissent. Notably, no member of the Court argued that Trump’s ballroom, an enormous structure that the president plans to build on the former site of the White House’s East Wing, is legal. As Roberts points out in dissent, a federal law prohibits the construction of any “building or structure … on any reservation, park, or public grounds of the Federal Government in the District of Columbia without express authority of Congress.” And, as Roberts writes, “Congress has not passed any law resembling ‘express authority’ for the Executive’s construction of” Trump’s ballroom. Email (required) Sign Up By submitting your email, you agree to our Terms and Privacy Notice . This site is protected by reCAPTCHA and the Google Privacy Policy and Terms of Service apply. Nevertheless, the five Republicans in the majority manage to rule in favor of Trump by effectively immunizing his ballroom from federal lawsuits. Their opinion highlights two of the most troubling things about the current Supreme Court: its reluctance to impose limits on Trump’s imperial-style presidency, and the frequent incoherence of its reasoning, especially in Trump cases. Their opinion suggests that no one is allowed to sue to challenge Trump’s decision to destroy and replace much of the White House. But it is short, does not explain key points of its argument, and relies on several distinctions that do not make any sense. As a general rule, no one is allowed to file a federal lawsuit unless they can show that they were injured in some way by the defendant they are suing — a requirement known as “standing.” But the Court has long held that plaintiffs suing under conservationist laws that seek to preserve a pristine, sacred, historical, or otherwise beautiful site have standing to bring a suit enforcing such laws against defendants who would damage or destroy such a site’s beauty. In Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife (1992), for example, the Court said that “the desire to use or observe an animal species, even for purely esthetic purposes, is undeniably a cognizable interest” that can be asserted in federal court. Similarly, the Court held in Friends of the Earth v. Laidlaw Environmental Services (2000) that “environmental plaintiffs adequately allege injury in fact when they aver that they use the affected area and are persons ‘for whom the aesthetic and recreational values of the area will be lessened’ by the challenged activity.’” So that’s how standing worked right up until Monday afternoon, when the Court handed down its latest opinion. The new rule is…well, it is difficult to parse. The plaintiff in National Park Service is a conservationist organization whose members include a retired professor who would frequently walk by the White House and who admired its beauty. Under decisions like Lujan and Friends of the Earth , that was enough to give her standing to sue in order to challenge the ballroom. The five Republicans in the majority, however, falsely claim that this individual merely argued that she is offended by Trump’s construction project, and that past decisions have involved “more than mere offense.” The Republicans note that, in Friends of the Earth , the plaintiffs not only wanted to view a river, but also to fish and swim in it and to camp nearby. But they don’t really even attempt to distinguish Lujan beyond a vague statement that Lujan requires a plaintiff’s injury to be “concrete and particularized.” Thus, because the majority opinion is so poorly explained, it is hard to tell what its implications will be. If the Court had explicitly overruled its past decisions holding that a plaintiff may often sue to challenge the destruction of something beautiful, that would be an existential threat to countless environmental, conservationist, and historical preservation laws that all exist to preserve natural or historic beauty. But the Court’s failure to explain why Lujan does not require them to rule against Trump leaves lawyers and judges to guess at what the Court just did to the rules governing standing. Perhaps this is a one-off decision intended solely to do a favor for Trump. Or maybe it’s the harbinger of a future decision setting much of America’s environmental protection regime on fire . The five justices in the majority barely explain themselves, so we cannot yet know what National Park Service means. But one thing that is clear is that the decision makes no sense. As Roberts writes in dissent, “it now is the case that ‘I want to look at a crocodile’ can adequately answer the ever-critical ‘what’s it to you?’ question of Article III standing, while ‘I want to look at the White House’ cannot.” But the justices in the majority couldn’t even be bothered to explain why. ##段落
政治 最高法院刚刚给了特朗普他的非法舞厅 而大法官们甚至懒得解释为什么……作者：伊恩·米尔希瑟 2026年8月31日，晚上9:45 UTC 赠品 2026年5月19日，总统唐纳德·特朗普在原本是东翼的位置旁，就其提议的白宫舞厅向记者讲话。Chip Somodevilla/盖蒂图片社 伊恩·米尔希瑟是Vox的高级记者，专注于最高法院、美国宪法以及美国自由民主的衰退。他拥有杜克大学的法学博士学位，并著有关于最高法院的两本书。

##段落
唉，最高法院已经决定唐纳德·特朗普总统可以建造他的舞厅。国家公园管理局诉国家历史保护信托案中的裁决是5比4，共和党首席大法官约翰·罗伯茨加入了三位民主党大法官的反对意见。值得注意的是，法院没有任何成员认为特朗普的舞厅——总统计划在前白宫东翼旧址上建造的巨型建筑——是合法的。正如罗伯茨在反对意见中指出的，联邦法律禁止“在哥伦比亚特区联邦政府的任何保留地、公园或公共场地上，未经国会明确授权建造任何‘建筑或结构’。”而且，正如罗伯茨所写，“国会没有通过任何类似于‘明确授权’的法律，来允许行政部门建造”特朗普的舞厅。

##段落

##段落
尽管如此，多数派中的五位共和党人设法通过有效地使特朗普的舞厅免受联邦诉讼来支持特朗普。他们的意见凸显了当前最高法院最令人不安的两点：它不愿对特朗普帝国式总统任期施加限制，以及其推理经常缺乏连贯性，尤其是在特朗普相关案件中。他们的意见表明，没有人可以起诉质疑特朗普摧毁并替换白宫大部分建筑的决定。但该意见篇幅简短，没有解释其论证的关键点，并依赖于几个毫无意义的区分。

##段落
一般而言，除非原告能证明他们因所起诉的被告而以某种方式受到伤害，否则不允许提起联邦诉讼——这一要求被称为“诉讼资格”。但法院长期以来一直认为，根据旨在保护原始、神圣、历史或其他美丽地点的保护主义法律提起诉讼的原告，具有诉讼资格，可以提起执行此类法律以对抗会损害或摧毁该地点之美的被告。例如，在卢汉诉野生动物保护者案（1992）中，法院表示“

##段落
渴望使用或观察某一动物物种，即便是纯粹出于审美目的，也无疑是一种可认定的利益，可以在联邦法院中主张。同样，法院在“地球之友诉莱德劳环境服务公司”（2000年）一案中裁定，“环境原告在声称使用受影响区域，且是‘该区域审美与休闲价值因被质疑活动而降低’的人时，即充分指控了事实上的伤害。”这就是直到周一下午法院发布最新意见之前，诉讼资格（standing）的运作方式。而新规则……嗯，很难解读。

##段落
“国家公园服务案”中的原告是一个环保组织，其成员包括一位退休教授，她经常路过白宫并欣赏其美景。根据“卢汉案”和“地球之友案”等判决，这足以赋予她起诉以挑战舞厅建设项目的资格。然而，占多数的五位共和党法官错误地声称，该个人仅主张她对特朗普的建设项目感到冒犯，而过去的判决涉及“不仅仅是单纯的冒犯”。共和党人指出，在“地球之友案”中，原告不仅想观赏河流，还想在其中钓鱼、游泳并在附近露营。但他们甚至没有真正尝试区分“卢汉案”，只是模糊地表示“卢汉案”要求原告的伤害必须是“具体且特定的”。

##段落
因此，由于多数意见解释得如此糟糕，很难判断其影响将是什么。如果法院明确推翻了过去认定原告常可起诉以挑战破坏美的事物的判决，那将对无数旨在保护自然或历史美景的环境法、环保法和历史保护法构成生存威胁。但法院未能解释为何“卢汉案”不要求他们裁定特朗普败诉，这让律师和法官只能猜测法院刚刚对诉讼资格规则做了什么。

##段落
也许这是一个仅为了给特朗普帮忙而作出的临时性决定。又或者，它是未来判决的先兆，可能点燃美国大部分环境保护体系。占多数的五位法官几乎没有解释自己，所以我们尚无法知道“国家公园服务案”意味着什么。但有一点是明确的：这一判决毫无道理。正如罗伯茨在异议中所写，“现在的情况是，‘我想看鳄鱼’可以充分回答第三条诉讼资格中至关重要的‘关你什么事？’问题，而‘我想看白宫’却不行。”但占多数的法官们甚至懒得解释为什么。
